hook.text: A model that wins in a notebook is still just a file. To be a product, it needs features at request time, an answer inside a latency budget, and labels coming back to say whether it was right.

plan.text: Designing that system is this round. Seventeen questions: eleven worked through, then six quickly.

q1.text: Question one. Batch versus online inference, and how do you choose? Batch scores everything on a schedule and stores the answers, like every user's recommendations, overnight. It's cheap and simple, but stale, and it can't use anything known only at request time.

q1-online.text: Online scores each request as it arrives, behind a low-latency service. It's fresh and can use context, like what's in the cart right now, but you own the latency budget, the scaling and the uptime.

q1-choose.text: So choose by freshness and latency. A stored answer is only a lookup, so batch suits a heavy model on a tight budget, if yesterday's answer will do and every input is known in advance: you can't precompute a reply to a search nobody has typed yet. Many systems mix the two, with features cached in batch and light scoring online.

q2-in.text: Serving online brings this round's favorite bug.

q2.text: Question two. What is training-serving skew? A feature computed one way when the training set is built, and another way when the model serves: different code, different data, or different timing.

q2-sim.text: Simulate a fraud model whose most telling feature is the card's transactions in the past hour. Training builds it from the warehouse, where the current transaction is already logged, so the count includes it. The serving path counts before it's written. Off by one.

q2-result.text: Offline, the model catches sixty percent of held-out fraud. Served the same transactions with the serving count, it catches forty-two. In training, the count was never zero; in serving, it's zero six times in ten.

q2-silent.text: Nothing errors, and offline evaluation can't see it, because it used the training definition. So build every feature through one shared path, and compare logged serving features with the training ones.

q3.text: Questions three and four. What is a feature store, and why use one? And what are its offline and online stores?

q3-what.text: It's one place to define, store and serve features, for training and serving alike. Teams reuse vetted features instead of rewriting them, and one transformation backs both paths, which is the cure for question two.

q3-stores.text: Each value is written to two stores. The offline store, a warehouse or a lake of files, keeps the full history, to build training sets. The online store, a key-value database like Redis, keeps only the latest value, served in milliseconds.

q3-time.text: The follow-up is time. A training row from March needs each feature as it stood in March. Join today's value instead, and the model trains on the future. So training sets are built with point-in-time lookups: the last value before each row's timestamp.

q5-in.text: Next, the model has to answer quickly, for many people at once.

q5.text: Questions five and six. What is throughput versus latency in model serving, and how does request batching improve GPU throughput? Latency is one request's time, judged at the tail: the ninety-fifth or ninety-ninth percentile. Throughput is requests per second, across the system.

q5-gpu.text: One request leaves most of a GPU idle, and every pass has a fixed cost. In a simple cost model, a fixed cost per pass plus a little per request, a batch of thirty-two gets about eight times the throughput of one at a time, for four times the latency per pass. Past that, throughput flattens and latency keeps climbing.

q5-sim.text: Simulate one GPU on that model, at a thousand requests a second. One at a time, it finishes three hundred and twenty a second, so the line grows by six hundred and eighty every second. Taking whatever has queued, up to thirty-two at once, it keeps up: ninety-nine percent finish within about ten milliseconds.

q5-wait.text: Serving frameworks also wait a few milliseconds to fill a batch. At a hundred requests a second, a five-millisecond wait lifts the median from three milliseconds to eight. At low load, waiting is pure latency, so cap it. And once one GPU's batches are full, add replicas: more throughput, and no replica gets slower.

q7.text: Question seven. What is model quantization? Storing the weights in fewer bits: eight-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, or even four bits. The model gets smaller, moves less data through memory, and usually runs faster.

q7-run.text: Take a small neural network that reads handwritten digits. Its seventeen thousand weights take sixty-eight kilobytes as 32-bit floats, and it gets ninety-seven point eight percent of five hundred forty held-out digits right. Round every weight to eight bits, a quarter of the size, and not one answer changes.

q7-cliff.text: At four bits, an eighth of the size, accuracy still holds. At two, it collapses to twenty-nine percent.

q7-qat.text: Rounding a finished model is post-training quantization: simple, and often enough. For aggressive compression, quantization-aware training rounds during training, so the weights learn to tolerate it. Either way, compare answers, not just the average: at four bits, two answers changed, one fixed and one broken, and accuracy didn't move.

q8-in.text: Speed is half the job. The system also has to learn whether the model was right.

q8.text: Question eight. What is label collection, and how do feedback loops work? After launch, the label is the outcome the prediction led to: a click, a purchase, a confirmed fraud. Logging it beside the prediction closes the loop.

q8-risks.text: Three things bend that loop. Labels arrive late: a purchase days after the click. You only see outcomes the model let happen: a transaction it blocked never shows whether it was fraud. And its actions change the data it sees next.

q8-explore.text: So log what the model decided, not just the outcome, and keep a small random slice where it doesn't decide. Those outcomes are the only ones the model didn't choose.

q9.text: Question nine. Sketch a fraud detection ML system. Features first: the amount, the merchant category, time since the last transaction, device and location, and velocity, the card's transactions in the last hour and the last day.

q9-serve.text: The model is gradient boosting, which suits tabular data like this, or a neural network over the card's history. It runs online, at authorization, in under a hundred milliseconds, so the velocity counts come from the online store. Its threshold is set by cost: a missed fraud against a good customer declined.

q9-labels.text: Labels are chargebacks, confirmed fraud, and they arrive late. So train only on transactions old enough for their chargebacks to have landed, or fresh fraud is learned as honest.

q9-watch.text: Then monitor precision and recall as the labels arrive, and drift in the velocity features before they do.

q10.text: Questions ten and eleven. Sketch a recommendation or ranking system. And how do you handle the cold-start problem? The standard design is a funnel.

q10-retrieve.text: Retrieval, a light model searching embeddings for nearest neighbors, narrows millions of items to a few hundred candidates.

q10-rank.text: Ranking, a heavier model with rich cross features, scores each candidate's chance of a click or a purchase. Re-ranking applies business rules: diversity, freshness, promotions. Versions of the ranker are compared in A B tests on revenue or engagement.

q10-why.text: Two stages, because the heavy model's cost grows with every item it scores. Ten million items is twenty thousand times the work of five hundred, so it only ever sees the five hundred.

q10-cold.text: Cold start is a new user or item with no history, so collaborative filtering has nothing to embed. Fall back to content, like item metadata or preferences asked for at sign-up, or to what's popular. A hybrid blends both signals with learned weights.

q10-loop.text: And a new item that's never shown never earns the clicks that would get it shown: question eight's loop again. So give new items some exposure on purpose.

r-features.text: Offline features are computed in batch jobs over history, and are as fresh as the last run. Online features are computed at request time, looked up in the online store or built from the request itself, like how recent the session is. Keeping the two definitions identical is the hard part.

r-validate.text: Data validation checks each new batch for schema, ranges, distributions and completeness before training. Without it, a new null column or a sensor that changes units trains a model on corrupt data, and it quietly underperforms.

r-gpu.text: GPUs win on large, parallel work: batched neural networks, transformers, images and video. For a light model, like a tree ensemble scoring one request, a CPU is faster, because the GPU's launch overhead would dominate.

r-distill.text: Knowledge distillation trains a small student to match a large teacher's probabilities, not just the labels. Shown one held-out nine, our digit network says sixty-five percent nine, thirty-five percent three. That tells a student nines can look like threes; the hard label says only nine.

r-latency.text: To cut serving latency, find where the time goes, then pull these levers: a compressed model, batching under load, a cache for repeated inputs, a faster runtime or hardware, the model placed beside its callers, and a simpler model on the paths that can't wait.

r-scale.text: And under variable load, autoscale replicas on utilization or queue depth. New replicas take time to warm up, so a request queue in front lets a spike wait instead of being dropped.

close.text: Features in, predictions out, labels back: that's the system around the model.

next.text: Once it's live, the world it learned from keeps changing. Next: shipping and monitoring models.
